name: Chlormadinone acetate

lead: Chlormadinone acetate is a prescription progestin with antiandrogenic effects, mainly found in combined contraceptive pills (such as Belara) sold outside the US. Doctors use these pills for women with acne, oily skin or hirsutism who also want contraception.
Acne evidence in the sources reviewed comes from open-label studies; no large randomized acne trial was found.

paras: It activates the progesterone receptor, blocks the androgen receptor and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering androgen effects in skin and hair follicles.

Low-dose pills commonly cause irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. High doses have been linked to adrenal and metabolic effects, and prolonged high-dose use to meningioma. It is prescription-only and was withdrawn in the US around 1970 after dog mammary tumour findings.

lead: Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin derived from 17-hydroxyprogesterone. It has progestogenic activity together with antiandrogenic effects, acting both by blocking the androgen receptor and by lowering gonadotropin-driven hormone production.[1][2] It is mostly used at 2 mg in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol (for example Belara), in some menopausal hormone therapies, and at higher doses for prostate conditions in Japan and South Korea.[1][2]

In the appearance context it is used in pills prescribed to women with acne, seborrhea, hirsutism or female pattern hair loss, similarly to cyproterone acetate.[1][2] Grokipedia reports open-label studies of an ethinylestradiol/CMA pill in mild to moderate papulopustular acne over 12 cycles.[2]
It is not marketed in the United States. Reports of meningioma with prolonged high-dose use of related progestins have prompted regulatory attention in Europe.[2]

paras: Wikipedia lists acne, hirsutism, seborrhea and pattern hair loss among androgen-dependent conditions for which CMA has been used in women.[1] Grokipedia describes EE/CMA studies reporting reductions in acne severity and oiliness over 12 treatment cycles in women aged 16 to 45, and use in hyperandrogenic conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.[2] A 2003 review of systemic acne treatment discusses antiandrogenic hormonal options in this area.[3]

CMA at 2 mg with 0.02 or 0.03 mg ethinylestradiol is a contraceptive, with reported adjusted Pearl indices from about 0.04 to 0.33.[2] It is also used in menopausal hormone therapy, in gynaecological disorders (for example in France as Luteran), and for prostate cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia mainly in Japan and South Korea.[1][2]

With low-dose combined pills, Wikipedia lists menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea, breast tenderness and vaginal discharge.[1] At high doses, sexual dysfunction, reduced body hair, adrenal insufficiency and altered carbohydrate metabolism have been reported, and with estrogen in menopausal therapy breast cancer risk is increased.[1] CMA is a teratogen in animals.[1]

Grokipedia states that epidemiological evidence has associated prolonged high-dose CMA exposure with an elevated risk of meningioma, similar to other progestins, and that CMA was withdrawn from the US market around 1970 after beagle dog studies linked it to mammary tumours, a finding not consistently seen in other species or in human data.[1][2] A registered retrospective cohort study (RIVET) has examined venous thromboembolism risk with hormonal contraceptives in about 124,000 participants.[4]

CMA is a progesterone receptor agonist, an androgen receptor antagonist (with weak partial agonism) and an antigonadotropin that suppresses LH and FSH; it has weak glucocorticoid activity and no estrogenic or antimineralocorticoid activity.[1] A 1988 laboratory study compared the androgenic activity of several synthetic progestins in mouse cells, and reviews classify CMA among progestogens with antiandrogenic properties.[5][6][7] Per Wikipedia, oral bioavailability is close to 100 percent and the elimination half-life roughly 25 to 89 hours.[1]

CMA was discovered in 1959 and introduced for medical use in 1965; Eli Lilly sold it with mestranol as C-Quens in the US from 1965 to 1971, and some countries withdrew it around 1970 over mammary tumours in beagle dogs, which later research did not find in humans.[1] Grokipedia dates its first synthesis to 1961.[2]

Brand names include Belara (Germany, Brazil), Gynorelle, Luteran (France), Lutoral (Mexico), Prostal (Japan) and Prostal-L (South Korea).[1] It is prescription-only. Environmental studies have detected progestogens including CMA in aquatic environments.[8][9] No community discussion sources were reviewed for this entry.

Registered trials in the sources reviewed include a comparison of body weight change during contraception with Belara versus Yasmin, a safety study of hormonal contraceptives in polycystic ovary syndrome, a postmenopausal hormone therapy study of progestagen type and gene expression, and a large retrospective venous thromboembolism cohort.[4][10][11][12] A review of hormonal contraceptives for dysmenorrhea also covers this drug class.[13] The acne findings summarised above come from secondary descriptions of open-label studies; no randomized acne trial was among the sources reviewed.
